title: Main ideas and summaries
intro: Find the whole point, not just an interesting detail.

sections.heading: Make a three-part map
body: Read once for the big change. Give the beginning, middle, and ending a few words each.
Join those notes. The main idea must cover the whole passage.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The school garden first sold all its vegetables. Students then noticed that some neighbors could not afford them. They kept the Saturday sales but set aside a free basket each morning. Sales now paid for seeds, while the baskets helped nearby families.

Question: Which map follows the whole passage?
A. Sell vegetables → notice a need → keep sales and add free food
B. Grow vegetables → lose every customer → close the garden
C. Give away seeds → start a shop → stop helping neighbors

Supported answer: Sell vegetables → notice a need → keep sales and add free food

Reason: “Kept the Saturday sales” and “set aside a free basket” show the two parts of the new plan.
Trap: The garden changes how it shares food; it does not close or stop selling.

sections.heading: Name the subject, then the point
body: Ask: What is this about? Then: What does the writer say about it?
A topic names the subject. A main idea explains the point.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
A library put its most borrowed books near the front door. Readers found them faster, but the narrow entrance became crowded. Staff moved the shelf beside the help desk. The books remained easy to find, and the doorway was clear again.

Question: Which choice gives the main idea?
A. The passage is about library shelves.
B. Moving a popular shelf solved an access problem while keeping books easy to find.
C. Putting every book near the door makes a library easier to use.

Supported answer: Moving a popular shelf solved an access problem while keeping books easy to find.

Reason: The first move helps readers but crowds the door. The second keeps the benefit and fixes the problem.
Trap: “Library shelves” is only the topic. “Every book” claims more than this one shelf shows.

sections.heading: Keep the beginning, turn, and ending
body: Look for a change: At first __. Then __. In the end __.
A good summary keeps that change. It does not stop at the first idea.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Jon thought restoring the old boat meant making it look new. While sanding, he found marks showing where earlier owners had repaired it. He left some marks visible and added a label explaining them. The boat could sail again, and visitors could see part of its history.

Question: Which summary follows Jon’s change?
A. He starts a repair but leaves the boat unable to sail.
B. He learns that old repairs should always be removed.
C. He begins by seeking a new appearance, then preserves useful signs of the past.

Supported answer: He begins by seeking a new appearance, then preserves useful signs of the past.

Reason: Jon starts with “making it look new” but later “left some marks visible.” Both parts belong in the summary.
Trap: Leaving marks does not mean abandoning the repair: the ending says the boat can sail.

sections.heading: Keep the answer within the evidence
body: Check who, where, and how sure. Keep the passage’s limits.
Watch words such as all, always, and proves. They need strong support.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Twenty volunteers tried a new bus route for one week. Most said it shortened their trip to work. The planner called the result encouraging but asked for a winter trial before changing the route permanently. No other riders had been surveyed.

Question: Which summary stays within the passage?
A. A short volunteer trial looks promising, but more testing is needed.
B. The new route will shorten every rider’s trip throughout the year.
C. The planner found no useful information in the trial.

Supported answer: A short volunteer trial looks promising, but more testing is needed.

Reason: “Twenty volunteers,” “one week,” and “before changing ... permanently” keep the result small and unfinished.
Trap: Encouraging does not mean proven for everyone. Asking for more testing does not mean the first trial was useless.

sections.heading: Show a character’s actual change
body: Compare what the person does at the start and end.
Name only the change those actions show. One brave act does not erase every fear.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
At her first rehearsal, Eva hid her drawing behind a folder when the director asked for costume ideas. A week later, she still felt nervous, but she put the drawing on the table and explained one part. Her hands shook while she spoke.

Question: What change does the passage show?
A. Eva stops caring about the costumes.
B. Eva shares an idea despite still feeling nervous.
C. Eva becomes completely confident in every situation.

Supported answer: Eva shares an idea despite still feeling nervous.

Reason: She first hides the drawing, then puts it on the table. Her shaking hands show that the nerves remain.
Trap: The ending supports a brave action, not the disappearance of all fear.

sections.heading: Settle the difference between two choices
body: When two answers seem close, name their difference.
Return to the line that settles that difference instead of rereading everything.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The museum offered a free evening opening. More visitors came, but only during the school holiday. Staff kept the evening for another month to see whether attendance stayed high after classes resumed. They had not yet decided on a permanent schedule.

Question: Which detail rules out “The evening opening is a proven year-round success”?
A. The opening was free.
B. The building was a museum.
C. The trial had only run during a school holiday.

Supported answer: The trial had only run during a school holiday.

Reason: “Only during the school holiday” leaves other parts of the year untested. That is the difference the answer must preserve.
Trap: A free opening may help attendance, but its price does not prove what will happen all year.

sections.heading: Repair a main-idea mistake
body: Name your mistake: too small, too broad, or missing the change.
Write a one-sentence summary with a detail from the start and end. Then try new text.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Lena expected the repair club to have an expert who knew every answer. Instead, members tested ideas together and sometimes failed. She returned the next week with a broken lamp and a notebook. She wanted to help test the next idea.

Question: Why is “Lena finds an expert who knows every repair” a poor summary?
A. It gives too much detail about the lamp.
B. It keeps her first expectation and ignores what she learns.
C. It correctly describes how the club works.

Supported answer: It keeps her first expectation and ignores what she learns.

Reason: “Instead” marks the turn: members test ideas and sometimes fail. Her return shows that she accepts that way of learning.
Trap: Do not summarize an early belief as if the rest of the passage confirmed it.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The passage’s main idea is that the restoration:
choices: refuses every change to the original building
proves photographs make all demolition harmless
focuses exclusively on increasing ticket prices
combines practical safety changes with attention to historical evidence
check.explanation: Both safe access and preserved or documented history are emphasized; neither aim displaces the other. The supported answer is “combines practical safety changes with attention to historical evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: During a restoration, the town replaced unsafe stairs but preserved the old doorway and photographed each change. The project’s report described the building as usable again without treating its history as an obstacle.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The passage primarily traces Ravi’s discovery that:
choices: questions prevent anyone from repairing objects
radios are simpler than every other device
learning repair can involve shared uncertainty and experimentation
experts never make mistakes
check.explanation: His initial image changes after seeing collaborative trial and error, and he returns ready to participate. The supported answer is “learning repair can involve shared uncertainty and experimentation.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Ravi expected the repair club to be a place where experts worked silently. Instead, members asked one another questions, tried solutions that failed, and laughed about familiar mistakes. He returned the following week with a broken radio and a list of questions.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The best summary is that organizers:
choices: cancel the park because outdoor festivals are unpopular
use an initial survey while seeking evidence from a broader group
discard every response as dishonest
have established every resident’s preferences
check.explanation: The group retains useful limited evidence and expands the inquiry rather than claiming complete representation. The supported answer is “use an initial survey while seeking evidence from a broader group.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: A survey showed interest in a new park, but responses came mainly from people attending an outdoor festival. Organizers kept the results, labeled the respondent group, and sought additional views before choosing facilities.

title: Details, sequence, and cause
intro: Find the exact fact and keep its meaning.

sections.heading: Find where the fact lives
body: Use a name, place, or action from the question to find the right part.
Read that sentence and its neighbor. You do not need to memorize every detail.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The class visited the river in April to collect water. In May, students tested the samples at school. They wrote their report in June and showed it to families in July. The teacher kept a copy beside the laboratory sink.

Question: Where should you look to find when the samples were tested?
A. The sentence about the May work at school
B. The sentence about the April river visit
C. The sentence about showing families the report

Supported answer: The sentence about the May work at school

Reason: “In May, students tested the samples” matches the exact action in the question.
Trap: Collecting and testing are different steps. A nearby date is not enough unless it belongs to the requested action.

sections.heading: Match the exact person or event
body: Turn the question into a small search: Who did what, and when?
Match all of those parts before choosing. A true detail can answer the wrong question.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
On Monday, Amir measured the stage. On Tuesday, Bea ordered boards using his measurements. Chen painted the boards on Friday, after the team had built the frame. The teacher checked the finished frame before the students carried it outside.

Question: Who ordered the boards?
A. Amir
B. Bea
C. Chen

Supported answer: Bea

Reason: “Bea ordered boards” supplies both the person and the action. The timing is Tuesday.
Trap: Amir measured; Chen painted. Both names are in the passage, but neither did the requested job.

sections.heading: Track what happened, when, and why
body: For order, follow before, after, and the named events.
For why, find the stated reason or connect the person’s action to a nearby clue.
After alone does not prove because. Keep the explanation within the text.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
On Monday, the club invited members to read a poem aloud. When his name was called, Nico studied the noticeboard instead of stepping forward. The next week, he practiced with one friend before joining the group reading.

Question: Why does Nico most likely study the noticeboard when called?
A. He is looking for the date of the next meeting.
B. He is avoiding the invitation to read aloud.
C. The club has asked him to repair the board.

Supported answer: He is avoiding the invitation to read aloud.

Reason: His name is called, but he looks away instead of stepping forward. Later practice with one friend supports difficulty joining the reading.
Trap: The passage never gives him a date-search or repair task. Use the action and its timing, not an invented reason.

sections.heading: Keep the number attached to what it counts
body: Read the noun beside the number: visits, people, items, or days.
Keep the group and time period too. Visits are not always different people.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The pool recorded 90 entries on Saturday. Some swimmers left for lunch and entered again, so each person could appear more than once in the count. Staff did not record names and could not tell how many different swimmers had attended.

Question: What does 90 count?
A. Entries into the pool
B. Different swimmers
C. Swimmers who stayed all day

Supported answer: Entries into the pool

Reason: The passage calls the number “90 entries” and says the same person could enter more than once.
Trap: Do not replace entries with people. The missing names prevent a count of different swimmers.

sections.heading: Change the words, keep the meaning
body: A paraphrase says the same thing in new words.
Check the actor, action, and limit. Similar words can still change the claim.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The coach supported adding one extra practice if players could still finish their schoolwork. She did not approve a daily increase. Before setting a date, she asked the team about homework deadlines and the hours they already spent traveling.

Question: Which choice restates the coach’s view?
A. She wants more practice every day.
B. She supports one extra practice only if schoolwork can still be completed.
C. She opposes any change to the schedule.

Supported answer: She supports one extra practice only if schoolwork can still be completed.

Reason: “If players could still finish their schoolwork” is a condition, so the restatement must keep it.
Trap: Support with a condition is neither full rejection nor approval of a daily increase.

sections.heading: Check the one detail that differs
body: If two choices differ by a name, date, or unit, compare that detail with the text.
Skip unrelated parts of the passage while settling this question.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The club collected coats in October and sorted them in November. The first delivery reached the shelter in December. A second delivery followed in January because several donors brought more coats after the original collection had ended.

Question: Which date answers “When did the first delivery arrive?”
A. October
B. January
C. December

Supported answer: December

Reason: “The first delivery reached the shelter in December” directly settles both first and arrived.
Trap: October belongs to collection. January belongs to the second delivery. Keep the requested event attached to its date.

sections.heading: Fix the exact mismatch
body: After a miss, name the part you changed: person, event, date, number, or condition.
Write the correct fact in one short sentence. Use that same check on the next passage.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
A theater counted 40 occupied seats before the interval and 35 afterward. The report did not record who sat in each seat. Sam summarized the report as “Only 35 different people attended the whole show,” but the counts cannot establish that.

Question: What did Sam change?
A. He changed occupied seats at one time into different people across the whole show.
B. He changed 35 into 40.
C. He changed a theater into a cinema.

Supported answer: He changed occupied seats at one time into different people across the whole show.

Reason: The report measures seats at two moments. It does not track each person across the show.
Trap: The number 35 is copied correctly, but copying a number does not preserve what it counts.

check.subject: reading
choices: Only after the June meeting ended
Before participants submitted any questions
After questions were submitted and before the June meeting
Before the April workshop was announced
check.explanation: The stated sequence is April workshop, submitted questions, revised handout, June meeting. The supported answer is “After questions were submitted and before the June meeting.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The first workshop met in April. Participants submitted questions before a second workshop in June, and the organizers revised the handout for the June meeting using those questions.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: What did the remaining cards directly count?
choices: All seeds passing above the cards
Seeds that struck their surfaces
Every seed leaving the trees
Only seeds later growing into plants
check.explanation: The first sentence defines the measured event, and the second explicitly excludes seeds passing above. The supported answer is “Seeds that struck their surfaces.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The collection cards counted seeds that struck their surfaces. Seeds passing above them were not counted, and two damaged cards were excluded from the report.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Which condition did the historian state?
choices: Retaining representative fixtures and recording alterations
Keeping dangerous wiring in active use
Removing every old fixture without notes
Closing the building to all visitors forever
check.explanation: The stated support is conditional on retained representative evidence and documentation. The supported answer is “Retaining representative fixtures and recording alterations.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The historian supported replacing dangerous wiring provided that representative old fixtures remained visible and the changes were recorded.

title: Evidence-based inference
intro: Use a clue to make one small, supported conclusion.

sections.heading: Use clues, not a new story
body: An inference is an idea the text supports without saying it directly.
Point to a clue. Then choose the answer that needs the fewest extra assumptions.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
When the audience began clapping, Noor remained beside the wings with her program folded in her hand. A loose page lay beneath the last violinist’s chair. While other visitors moved toward the exit, she kept looking at the page.

After the players had left, she crossed the stage and picked it up. Outside, she caught up with the violinist and handed it over without introducing herself or mentioning the applause.

Question: Which inference about Noor’s reason for remaining has the clearest evidentiary link?
A. She wants the audience to recognize her role in the performance.
B. She remains at least partly so she can return the fallen page.
C. She and the violinist had arranged beforehand for her to collect the page.

Supported answer: She remains at least partly so she can return the fallen page.

Reason: Noor keeps looking at the page, then picks it up and returns it. Those linked actions support a reason for waiting.
Trap: We do not know her only motive. The text gives no clue of a plan made earlier or a wish for applause.

sections.heading: Build one small link from the clue
body: Use this sentence: The text says __, so __ is likely.
Stop there. Do not add a motive, event, or future success the text does not support.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The town’s archive normally closed at four. Ravi arrived at five, found the door locked, and photographed the opening-hours sign. He walked away without trying another entrance. The sign listed a Saturday opening that would fit around his weekday work.

Question: What is the best supported inference?
A. Ravi may return when the archive is open.
B. Ravi owns the archive.
C. Ravi has decided to stop researching.

Supported answer: Ravi may return when the archive is open.

Reason: Photographing useful opening hours gives him information for a later visit. That is a small link from his action.
Trap: Ownership and quitting are extra stories. The locked door alone does not prove either one.

sections.heading: Choose what the text supports
body: “Could happen” is weaker than “this text gives a reason to expect it.”
Ask which detail supports the answer. A possible story without a clue is not enough.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
A pilot ferry ran for two summer weekends. Most seats were filled. The council paid for an autumn trial before deciding whether to run it all year. No winter trips had taken place, and the council had made no permanent funding decision.

Question: Which conclusion has evidence behind it?
A. The ferry will certainly run all winter.
B. The council thinks more testing is worthwhile.
C. The council believes the summer trial failed completely.

Supported answer: The council thinks more testing is worthwhile.

Reason: Paying for another trial shows interest in learning more. “Before deciding” keeps the permanent decision open.
Trap: Full summer boats do not prove winter demand. Continuing the test also does not show total rejection.

sections.heading: Read feelings from words and actions
body: Look at what the person says and does. Both are clues.
Match how strong the feeling is. A worry is not always a refusal.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
“The new trail could be wonderful,” Jo said, studying the map. She then asked whether its steep bridge would be repaired before opening day. She offered to help mark the route once the bridge was safe enough for the walking group.

Question: How does Jo feel about the trail?
A. She rejects the whole project.
B. She has no concerns about it.
C. She is interested but concerned about one condition.

Supported answer: She is interested but concerned about one condition.

Reason: “Could be wonderful” and the offer to help show interest. The bridge question supplies the concern.
Trap: One worry does not cancel all support, and praise does not erase the safety condition.

sections.heading: Try to disprove the tempting answer
body: Ask: If this answer were true, what else would have to be true?
Check that claim against the passage. One clear contradiction can eliminate it.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Leah disliked the first draft of the group’s poster because its lettering was hard to read. She kept the drawing, enlarged the title, and asked to display the new draft at lunch. She made no request to leave the group.

Question: What most challenges the claim that Leah abandoned the project?
A. She disliked the first draft.
B. She improved the poster and asked to display it.
C. The first title was small.

Supported answer: She improved the poster and asked to display it.

Reason: Improving and displaying the poster show continued work on the project. Those actions conflict with abandoning it.
Trap: Disliking one draft is not the same as rejecting the whole project.

sections.heading: Find the clue that settles the choice
body: For two close answers, say what each would require.
Return to one useful action or sentence. Do not fill a gap with your own guess.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
When the borrowed violin made a faint sound, Jae first blamed the instrument. His teacher played one clear note on it. Jae then changed the way he held the bow and tried again, listening carefully before making another adjustment.

Question: What most strongly supports “Jae is willing to change his approach”?
A. He borrowed a violin.
B. He initially blamed the instrument.
C. He changed his bow hold and tried again.

Supported answer: He changed his bow hold and tried again.

Reason: The changed bow hold is an action that directly supports a changed approach.
Trap: Borrowing says nothing about flexibility. His first complaint describes the earlier attitude, before he tried a different method.

sections.heading: Remove the unsupported leap
body: After a miss, name what you added: a motive, a certainty, or a future event.
Replace it with a smaller claim and point to the clue that supports it.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
After tasting the soup, Nia asked for the recipe and wrote down the ingredients. She said she wanted to try it at home on Sunday. Her friend concluded that she planned to open a restaurant, although Nia had said nothing about selling food.

Question: Which conclusion repairs the unsupported leap?
A. Nia wants to make the soup at home.
B. Nia has already opened a restaurant.
C. Nia dislikes all other recipes.

Supported answer: Nia wants to make the soup at home.

Reason: “Try it at home on Sunday” supports cooking the soup at home. It does not establish a business plan.
Trap: Keep the stated plan. Asking for ingredients does not by itself show a career decision or a dislike of other food.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Jules’s actions most reasonably suggest a wish to:
choices: end the museum’s use of maps altogether
preserve the original project while broadening the evidence
prove the first interviewees invented their memories
make the second map identical to the first
check.explanation: Keeping and relabeling the first map documents it; inviting absent groups expands participation. The supported answer is “preserve the original project while broadening the evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Jules left the original map on display, added a caption naming its interview group, and invited previously absent neighborhoods to contribute to a second map.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The office most likely believes that:
choices: the promising trend still needs testing under different conditions
the trial has proved year-round demand beyond doubt
summer programs never affect attendance
further observations are unnecessary
check.explanation: Extending the trial while changing the seasonal context shows qualified interest rather than certainty. The supported answer is “the promising trend still needs testing under different conditions.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: After seeing a rise in attendance, the office extended the trial into another season and asked whether riders would use the service when the summer program ended.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Amira’s response is best described as:
choices: entirely hostile from beginning to end
proof she no longer wants to rehearse
certain that every interruption is beneficial
mixed initially, with later recognition of a useful result
check.explanation: The text combines enjoyment and concern, then supplies one specific benefit without a universal claim. The supported answer is “mixed initially, with later recognition of a useful result.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Amira enjoyed the group’s spontaneous song but worried about the rehearsal time it used. Later she tried a phrase suggested during that exchange and found it helped.

title: Words in context
intro: Let the surrounding words tell you the meaning.

sections.heading: Read around the word
body: Find the word in the passage. Read its sentence and the sentence beside it.
Ask what it means here, not what it usually means elsewhere.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The review called the set spare. The stage held one chair and a small lamp; no curtains, painted scenery, or other furniture surrounded them. The reviewer said this simple arrangement kept attention on the actor’s words.

Question: Which meaning of “spare” fits this set?
A. An extra one kept for later
B. Simple, with little decoration
C. To save someone from harm

Supported answer: Simple, with little decoration

Reason: “One chair and a small lamp” plus the missing scenery show a simple set with few objects.
Trap: An extra supply is a familiar meaning of spare, but no backup set is described here.

sections.heading: Make a plain-word replacement
body: Cover the choices and replace the word with a simple phrase.
Then choose the answer closest to your phrase. Read it back in the sentence.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The board’s support was guarded. Members agreed to fund one trial, but they wanted to see the results before paying for a larger project. Their letter welcomed the idea while making clear that future funding was still undecided.

Question: What does “guarded” mean here?
A. Cautious
B. Protected by a security officer
C. Completely opposed

Supported answer: Cautious

Reason: The board funds a trial but waits before making a larger promise. Replace guarded with cautious.
Trap: The topic is support, not physical security. Funding a trial also rules out complete opposition.

sections.heading: Use the clue beside the word
body: Look for a contrast, example, or explanation nearby.
Words such as but, rather than, and unlike often show which meaning fits.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Unlike the first speaker’s long, winding answer, Tessa’s reply was succinct. She named the problem in one sentence and suggested a solution in the next. The chair thanked her for making the point easy to follow.

Question: What does “succinct” mean?
A. Hard to understand
B. Brief and clear
C. Quiet enough to be missed

Supported answer: Brief and clear

Reason: The contrast with “long, winding” and the two-sentence reply point to brief and clear.
Trap: The passage discusses length and clarity. It gives no evidence that Tessa spoke softly.

sections.heading: Notice when a word makes a picture
body: Some words describe an idea as if it were a physical thing.
Ask what is actually changing. Keep the comparison’s meaning without taking it literally.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
For years, Owen believed every repair had one perfect method. After watching three skilled builders solve the same problem differently, his certainty began to loosen. He still worked carefully, but he was more willing to try another approach.

Question: What does “loosen” mean here?
A. Come untied like a rope
B. Disappear completely
C. Become less fixed

Supported answer: Become less fixed

Reason: Owen becomes more willing to try another approach, so his belief is less fixed.
Trap: No rope is involved, and he does not lose every belief or stop working carefully.

sections.heading: Check the word against the whole point
body: A replacement must fit both the sentence and the point around it.
Reject a meaning that fits the general topic but changes this particular claim.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The scientist called the estimate provisional. It used the measurements available that morning, and the team expected to revise it after a second visit. The report showed the current figure clearly but warned readers against treating it as a final total.

Question: Which replacement keeps the writer’s point?
A. Open to revision
B. Kept secret
C. Known to be false

Supported answer: Open to revision

Reason: “Expected to revise it” directly explains provisional. The estimate may change as more evidence arrives.
Trap: A possible revision does not mean the current estimate is deliberately hidden or already disproved.

sections.heading: Test only the useful meanings
body: When a word has several meanings, test the ones that fit its job in this sentence.
Substitute one at a time. Keep the meaning that preserves the writer’s point.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The notice said the path was closed. A fallen tree blocked the narrow bridge, and workers had placed a barrier at each end. Walkers were directed to the road until the trunk could be removed safely.

Question: Which meaning of “closed” fits the notice?
A. Finished for the day, like a meeting
B. Not available for passage
C. Drawn close together, like curtains

Supported answer: Not available for passage

Reason: The barriers and directions to another route show that people cannot use the path.
Trap: Other meanings of closed are real, but only one describes access to this blocked route.

sections.heading: Save the clue, not just a definition
body: After a miss, write down the nearby words that decided the meaning.
Use the word in a new sentence with the same meaning. Then try a different word in context.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The curator said the note was pertinent to the date of the painting. It named the exhibition where the artist first showed it. Other letters described the artist’s meals but gave no information about when the work was made.

Question: Which clue shows that “pertinent” means relevant?
A. The note helps answer the question about the painting’s date.
B. The note is older than every other letter.
C. The artist enjoyed the meals described.

Supported answer: The note helps answer the question about the painting’s date.

Reason: Naming the first exhibition helps with the date question. That useful connection is what makes the note pertinent.
Trap: The passage does not rank the letters by age. Meal details are contrasted with evidence useful to the question.

check.subject: reading
choices: open to revision
guaranteed to be exact
kept secret permanently
unrelated to evidence
check.explanation: The explanation after the colon directly establishes that the estimate can change with measurements. The supported answer is “open to revision.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The report called the first estimate provisional: the team would revise it as new measurements arrived.

check.subject: reading
choices: inaudible
recently invented
deliberately false
relevant
check.explanation: The contrast links usefulness to the particular research question. The supported answer is “relevant.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The chair movement was distracting to a listener studying pitch, but pertinent to a historian studying the audience’s behavior.

check.subject: reading
choices: was entirely forgotten
became physically larger
became less strict
was tied more tightly
check.explanation: The change affects a rigid belief, and the continuing careful work rules out total abandonment. The supported answer is “became less strict.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Her rigid idea of rehearsal loosened after she saw that careful work could include questions and laughter.

title: Purpose, tone, and structure
intro: Notice why the writer chose a detail, voice, or image.

sections.heading: Ask why this detail is here
body: First say what the detail tells you. Then ask what job it does.
Does it give an example, explain a cause, challenge an idea, or show a change?

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The new mountain road appears as one continuous line joining the coastal town to the villages above it. At the opening, a council speaker called that line a connection for every home.

Rafi could drive his empty cart along the road, but with a full load of grain he stopped at its steepest turn. He carried several sacks around the bend before bringing the cart through.

A map can record a connection without showing the effort it demands from particular users. For Rafi, the road’s usefulness still depends on the cart’s load and the slope beneath its wheels.

Question:  Which structural map fits?
A. Claim about connection → concrete difficulty → qualification of what connection means
B. General claim about travel → proof that the road has no useful purpose → a replacement route
C. A farmer’s difficulty → an account of why he caused it → confirmation of the opening claim

Supported answer: Claim about connection → concrete difficulty → qualification of what connection means

Reason: Rafi must unload sacks at the turn. That real difficulty limits the speaker’s claim that the road connects every home equally.
Trap: The road is usable. The point is that its value depends on the load and slope.

sections.heading: Name the paragraph’s job
body: Read the paragraph with the one before and after it.
Finish this sentence: The writer includes this to __. A job is more than a topic.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Museum labels should help visitors learn about what they see. A clear label can answer a question without a guide standing nearby.

At one exhibit, however, a label used terms that a school group did not understand. Students left with the same questions they had brought.

Before printing a full set, staff should ask visitors to read sample labels and explain what they learned.

Question: What is the middle paragraph’s job?
A. Show why labels that aim to help still need testing
B. Give a complete history of the museum
C. Prove that every museum label is useless

Supported answer: Show why labels that aim to help still need testing

Reason: Students leave with unanswered questions. That problem explains why the last paragraph recommends testing labels with visitors.
Trap: One confusing label limits the opening claim; it does not prove that all labels fail.

sections.heading: Match the feeling and its strength
body: Tone means the writer’s attitude. Find words that show it.
Match both the feeling and how strong it is: worried is different from furious.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The play’s lively dialogue and strong lead performance make it worth seeing. The slow ending could still use another revision, but it does not spoil the evening. I recommend this production and look forward to the group’s next one.

Question: Which tone fits the whole review?
A. Angry and dismissive
B. Positive, with a small reservation
C. Unsure whether anything worked

Supported answer: Positive, with a small reservation

Reason: “Worth seeing” and “I recommend” show approval. The slow ending adds one criticism without reversing that approval.
Trap: Do not let one criticism erase the positive judgment across the rest of the review.

sections.heading: Track a speaker’s view and how it changes
body: Keep each speaker’s view separate from the author’s. Check the response after a quote.
For a change in viewpoint, compare the opening view with the later one.
Name what is added, challenged, or kept. A new view may extend an old one instead of rejecting it.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
“Machines have made the hand unnecessary,” a manufacturer announced at the fair. His advertisement showed the finished product sliding from a bright metal opening.

Behind the display, a worker paused the machine when its printed guide failed. She adjusted the feed wheel by touch, ran a test, and adjusted it again before allowing the product to continue.

The hand had not disappeared from this process. Which kinds of handwork, then, had the advertisement taught its visitors not to notice?

Question: Why does the essay include the manufacturer’s claim?
A. To introduce a position that the following observations complicate
B. To certify the claim as the essay’s own conclusion
C. To establish that the workers refused to use the machine

Supported answer: To introduce a position that the following observations complicate

Reason: The worker “adjusted the feed wheel by touch.” Her action shows that handwork is still needed after the manufacturer claims it is not.
Trap: A quote is not automatically the author’s view. Read what the author puts after it.

sections.heading: Explain what an image helps us notice
body: For a comparison, name the feature the two things share.
Connect that feature to the scene. Do not bring in every fact about the comparison.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
At dusk, the greenhouse windows glowed like small lanterns along the dark field. Mara slowed her walk to look at the rows of warm light. Inside, the gardeners were covering the youngest plants before the temperature dropped.

Question: What does the lantern comparison emphasize?
A. The windows’ warm light against the darkness
B. The greenhouse’s ability to fly
C. The exact temperature of each plant

Supported answer: The windows’ warm light against the darkness

Reason: The passage sets “glowed” and “warm light” against the “dark field.” That is the shared feature of windows and lanterns.
Trap: A comparison highlights a useful likeness. It does not give the greenhouse every property of another object.

sections.heading: Use two clues for tone
body: Check at least two words or actions before naming an attitude.
A sad subject does not automatically make the writer’s tone sad or angry.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Inspectors found loose joints on the town bridge. The east lane is closed while those joints are repaired. Work is scheduled to finish on Friday. Until then, drivers should follow the marked route through Mill Street and allow extra travel time.

Question: Which description fits the report’s tone?
A. Panicked because any damage is frightening
B. Calm and practical
C. Mocking the people who use the bridge

Supported answer: Calm and practical

Reason: The list of damage, repair schedule, and directions focus on facts and actions. They support a calm, practical tone.
Trap: Choose from the wording and treatment, not from how the damaged bridge makes you feel.

sections.heading: Separate what it says from what it does
body: After a purpose miss, write two notes: This says __. It helps the writer __.
Keep a speaker’s words separate from the author’s response.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Before leaving, I checked the forecast three times. The same chance of showers remained on the screen; I wanted a more cooperative answer. I finally put the phone away and hurried toward the club.

When rain began, I kept going. By the time I arrived, my sleeves were wet, my shoes made a noise on the floor, and I was laughing.

A student labels the first paragraph’s purpose “to tell us that the narrator checks the weather.”

Question: Which revision explains its role rather than repeating its content?
A. It contrasts the narrator’s early wish to avoid rain with the later laughter despite getting wet.
B. It establishes the checks as evidence that the later rain was forecast accurately.
C. It shows why reaching the club depends on obtaining a different forecast.

Supported answer: It contrasts the narrator’s early wish to avoid rain with the later laughter despite getting wet.

Reason: “I wanted a more cooperative answer” shows a wish to avoid rain. “I was laughing” shows a different response after getting wet.
Trap: Saying “checks the weather” names the action. The question asks how that action connects to the ending.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The festival detail mainly serves to:
choices: prove the attendance count was fabricated
explain why every resident opposes the route
show that further trials are impossible
qualify what the attendance increase can establish
check.explanation: The detail introduces a simultaneous influence that limits interpretation of the increase. The supported answer is “qualify what the attendance increase can establish.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Attendance increased during the trial. Yet the report noted that a festival took place at the same time and recommended another trial after the festival ended.

check.subject: reading
choices: why the singer never performed live
why all digital copies must be identical
why different sounds require different processing judgments
why every rough sound should be removed
check.explanation: The contrast concerns confidence about each sound’s source and the resulting restoration choice. The supported answer is “why different sounds require different processing judgments.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The engineer compared a surface click with the singer’s rough vocal edge. One could confidently be attributed to the recording medium; the other might belong to the performance.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The changing chair arrangements primarily reveal:
choices: an unchanged preference for appearances above use
a shift toward practical needs and shared use
a decision to end all musical work
evidence that every chair is damaged
check.explanation: The three arrangements trace a movement from image to function and acceptance of other room purposes. The supported answer is “a shift toward practical needs and shared use.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: At first the narrator arranged chairs symmetrically to make the room look serious. Later the narrator moved them to help the players see one another, then returned them for a family visit.

title: Paired texts and visual evidence
intro: Compare sources without changing what either one says.

sections.heading: Read each source on its own first
body: Write one short note for A and one for B. Keep any conditions.
Then compare them. Do not combine the views before you know what each says.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Writer A: Open the school garden on weekends so families can visit. Pupils can still grow food there during the week.

Writer B: I welcome weekend visitors too, but the youngest beds should be fenced first. Families could enjoy the paths while leaving those beds for the pupils to tend.

Question: Which pair of notes is accurate?
A. A: welcome visitors. B: welcome visitors after protecting the young beds.
B. A: close the garden. B: remove every bed.
C. A: stop growing food. B: keep families out forever.

Supported answer: A: welcome visitors. B: welcome visitors after protecting the young beds.

Reason: A supports weekend access. B agrees but adds “fenced first,” a condition on that access.
Trap: A condition is not total opposition. Both still support growing food during the week.

sections.heading: Find the agreement and the difference
body: Ask what both writers support. Then ask what one adds or changes.
A condition such as “only if” can be the main difference.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Writer A: The old hall should host community events again. A building that once brought neighbors together can do so once more if we reopen its doors.

Writer B: I support reopening only if the original painted ceiling is protected during repairs. We can welcome people back while keeping that part of the hall’s history.

Question: How does B’s view relate to A’s?
A. B opposes all public events.
B. B shares the goal and adds a condition about protecting the ceiling.
C. B proves that A wants the ceiling destroyed.

Supported answer: B shares the goal and adds a condition about protecting the ceiling.

Reason: Both support reopening. B’s “only if” adds a protection requirement that A does not mention.
Trap: Silence about the ceiling does not prove that A wants it damaged. Do not invent a disagreement.

sections.heading: Keep only what both sources support
body: Check each part of the answer against its evidence.
Within one passage, compare the two named moments: what stays, changes, or connects?
Across sources, keep both claims and their limits. Do not add a cause or promise neither source establishes.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
The library report says the evening opening brought in 30 visitors during its first week. The budget note says staff covered that week without extra pay, but future staffing costs are undecided. Neither source describes attendance after the first week.

Question: Which combined statement is supported?
A. Evening hours are guaranteed to stay free forever.
B. The opening failed because future costs are unknown.
C. The first week attracted visitors without extra pay, while later costs remain unsettled.

Supported answer: The first week attracted visitors without extra pay, while later costs remain unsettled.

Reason: The report supplies the visitors; the budget note supplies first-week pay and the limit on future costs.
Trap: Do not turn a successful first week into a permanent guarantee or an unknown cost into proof of failure.

sections.heading: Read the table’s labels, then compare
body: Read what each number counts. For a share, divide the part by the whole.
Then connect that result to the passage. A higher count can still be a smaller share.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
A club wants a larger share of members to attend. Before changing meeting time, 20 of its 40 members came. After the change, 30 of 100 members came. Membership also grew, so comparing only 20 and 30 would miss part of the picture.

Question: What happened to attendance?
A. The number rose, but the share fell from 50% to 30%.
B. Both the number and the share rose.
C. The share stayed the same because both counts are positive.

Supported answer: The number rose, but the share fell from 50% to 30%.

Reason: Before: 20 ÷ 40 = 50%. After: 30 ÷ 100 = 30%. More people came, but they were a smaller share of members.
Trap: Compare part ÷ whole. The raw counts 20 and 30 cannot answer a question about share.

sections.heading: Keep every source’s limits
body: Check who was measured and under which conditions.
A combined answer must keep the limits from all sources, even if a broader answer sounds useful.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
A survey reports that most of 15 volunteer cyclists liked a new sign. A separate report says the sign was tested on one route during daylight. Neither report counted accidents or included nighttime riders, and no other route was studied.

Question: Which conclusion stays within both reports?
A. The sign prevents accidents on every route.
B. The volunteers generally liked the sign in the limited setting tested.
C. Night riders disliked the sign.

Supported answer: The volunteers generally liked the sign in the limited setting tested.

Reason: The survey gives the volunteers’ opinion; the second report limits the setting to one daylight route.
Trap: Neither source measures accident prevention or night riders’ views. Do not fill in those missing results.

sections.heading: Check the exact overlap
body: When asked what both writers accept, find a line from each.
If only one source supports a choice, it cannot be the shared answer.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Writer A: We should copy the old recordings so more people can hear them. A copy can travel to listeners who cannot visit our archive.

Writer B: Copies do improve access. But we should also keep the originals available for future study. A researcher may someday need a detail that today’s copies do not preserve.

Question: What do both writers explicitly support?
A. Discarding every original
B. Replacing all future research with copies
C. Using copies to let more people hear the recordings

Supported answer: Using copies to let more people hear the recordings

Reason: A wants more people to hear the recordings. B agrees that copies improve access. Those two statements overlap.
Trap: Keeping originals is B’s added point. A’s silence does not make that point an explicit shared claim.

sections.heading: Find which source your answer changed
body: After a miss, check the answer against A, B, and any table separately.
Name the change: mixed up speakers, dropped a condition, or changed a number’s meaning.

examples.label: Point to the proof
examples.text:
Writer A: Let us try later bus service for one month. People leaving evening shifts could have another way home, and we could find out how many use it.

Writer B: I support that trial if the council checks its cost after the month. We need that information before deciding what comes next.

A student summarizes them as “Both promise that later service will be permanent.”

Question: What is wrong with the student’s summary?
A. It turns support for a trial into a promise of permanent service.
B. It correctly keeps B’s cost condition.
C. It shows that A opposes the trial.

Supported answer: It turns support for a trial into a promise of permanent service.

Reason: Both discuss a trial. B also requires a cost check, so permanent service is not an agreed promise.
Trap: Keep the type of commitment: trying an idea and committing to it forever are different claims.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Which claim would both writers most likely accept?
choices: Only the smoothest version should survive
Future listeners must ask today’s exact questions
A useful listening copy should be accompanied by access to evidence about its production
All processing is inherently unacceptable
check.explanation: A asks for inspectable changes; B asks for retained copies and notes. Both support usable presentations with evidence preserved. The supported answer is “A useful listening copy should be accompanied by access to evidence about its production.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context:
Passage A: A restored recording should be easier to hear, but listeners should be able to inspect changes.

Passage B: Public listening copies are useful, but institutions should retain original copies and notes so later researchers can ask different questions.

check.subject: reading
choices: The number of scheduled returns stayed the same
The on-time proportion increased, but the reminder’s separate effect is not isolated
The increase proves reminders alone caused every change
The later on-time proportion was 45 percent
check.explanation: The proportions are60percent and75percent; the simultaneous hours change limits causal attribution. The supported answer is “The on-time proportion increased, but the reminder’s separate effect is not isolated.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Before a reminder trial, 30 of 50 scheduled returns were on time. During the trial, 45 of 60 were on time. The report notes that opening hours also changed.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: How does B’s position relate to A’s?
choices: It shares support for use while adding conditions about historical evidence
It denies that anyone should enter the theater
It proves that every old mechanism is safe
It treats documentation as a replacement for all surviving features
check.explanation: B agrees about continued use and adds retained mechanisms plus documentation; that is a qualification, not total opposition. The supported answer is “It shares support for use while adding conditions about historical evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Passage A argues that public use helps a theater survive. Passage B supports continued use but asks that representative old stage mechanisms remain visible and alterations be documented.
